paragraphs: This paper explores whether a neural circuit modeled on a biological nervous system can be repurposed as a robot controller. The authors introduce ordinary neural circuits, or ONCs, inspired by the soil worm C. elegans. Their approach keeps a biologically motivated circuit structure while changing its parameters so that it can control alternative tasks.

The authors first show that these circuits have higher maximum network flow than arbitrarily wired networks. They then use a search-based optimization algorithm to configure ONCs for robotic control. The demonstrations include both simulated tasks and autonomous parking by a real rover, connecting the circuit design to physical control behavior.

In the reported comparisons, ONCs match contemporary deep learning controllers and significantly exceed their performance in some cases. They are also 77% sparser than the counterpart controllers, and the authors describe their neural dynamics as fully interpretable at the individual-cell level. Together, these findings suggest that biological circuit structure can provide a useful starting point for compact controllers whose internal dynamics can be examined.
icml-2020-a-natural-lottery-ticket-winne.tldr: Biologically inspired neural circuits provide compact, cell-level interpretable controllers that match or sometimes outperform contemporary deep learning models on robotic tasks.

paragraphs: Deep graph neural networks can overfit their training data or over-smooth their representations, making different nodes less distinguishable. This paper addresses both tendencies by learning how to sample graph connections during training. Its framework generalizes existing stochastic regularization approaches, which introduce randomness into the connections used by a network.

The central change is to train the sampling rates alongside the network parameters instead of fixing those rates or choosing them by hand. The framework supports both global and local adaptation. The authors also establish a mathematical equivalence between this training procedure and an efficient approximation to Bayesian graph neural network training, giving the connection sampling a role in learning with uncertainty.

Benchmark experiments and ablation studies support adaptive sampling as the key contributor to improved semi-supervised node classification. The reported models are less susceptible to over-smoothing and overfitting and produce more robust predictions. The contribution therefore connects a practical regularization decision—how often to retain connections—to a trainable mechanism with a Bayesian interpretation.
icml-2020-bayesian-graph-neural-networks.tldr: Learning connection-sampling rates jointly with a graph neural network improves reported classification performance and provides an approximate Bayesian treatment of uncertainty.

paragraphs: Controlling a humanoid requires coordinating a complex body, but useful control also means reusing learned movements in new situations. CoMic studies how to build reusable skills by combining imitation of motion capture recordings with reinforcement learning on complementary tasks. The goal is a collection of behaviors that supports more than accurate reproduction of recorded motion.

The authors show that reusable skills can be learned using 50 times as much motion capture data as prior work. They systematically compare several network architectures across different amounts of training data. These comparisons assess both imitation quality and transfer to challenging locomotion tasks, treating successful reuse as a separate concern from matching the original recordings.

The paper also shows that motion tracking can be interleaved with complementary task training. This enriches the learned skill space and enables reuse of behaviors poorly represented in the recordings, including getting up from the ground and catching a ball. The findings support combining recorded examples with task experience to extend the range of reusable humanoid behavior.
icml-2020-comic-complementary-task-learn.tldr: CoMic combines large-scale motion imitation with complementary task training to learn humanoid skills that can be reused beyond the recorded motions.

paragraphs: An untrained convolutional network can recover an image by fitting its parameters directly to measurements of that single image. This avoids the need for a separate training dataset. The paper examines why this approach can work in compressive sensing, where only a small number of measurements are available and many possible images could fit them.

The surprising property is that a network capable of representing any image can still recover a natural image when gradient descent runs to convergence. In this setting, the network and optimization procedure exhibit a form of self-regularization. This differs from some other recovery applications, where stopping optimization early is critical to obtaining useful results.

The authors provide numerical evidence and a theoretical study of this behavior. Their result shows that sufficiently structured signals and images can be approximately reconstructed from a near-minimal number of random measurements without additional regularization. The qualifications matter: the guarantee concerns approximate recovery of structured targets under random measurement, explaining a specific recovery setting rather than establishing unrestricted reconstruction from sparse observations.
icml-2020-compressive-sensing-with-un-tr.tldr: The paper explains how untrained convolutional networks can approximately recover sufficiently structured signals from few random measurements without additional regularization.

paragraphs: This paper learns representations of individual nodes and entire graphs through self-supervision. Its training signal comes from contrasting different structural views of the same graph. The central question is which views provide useful information for learning features that later support classification, without relying on classification labels to learn those features.

The strongest reported configuration contrasts an encoding based on immediate neighbors with one based on graph diffusion, which reflects connectivity beyond those immediate neighbors. In the authors’ experiments, adding more than two views or contrasting encodings across multiple scales does not improve performance. These findings identify a particular pairing as effective within the evaluated graph-learning setting.

Under linear evaluation, the method achieves the best reported self-supervised results on all eight node and graph classification benchmarks. It reaches 86.8% accuracy on Cora and 84.5% on Reddit-Binary, corresponding to relative improvements of 5.5% and 2.4%. It also exceeds supervised baselines on four benchmarks. The results show that carefully chosen structural views can yield features useful even to a linear classifier.
icml-2020-contrastive-multi-view-represe.tldr: Contrasting immediate-neighbor and diffusion views learns graph representations that achieve leading self-supervised results on all eight evaluated classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: Interactive Attention Learning lets a human correct model behavior by changing where the model allocates attention. This creates a practical challenge: attention feedback is scarce, retraining can be expensive, and people cannot inspect every feature of every example. The paper develops a framework that addresses both model adaptation and the cost of deciding what humans should review.

Its first component, Neural Attention Processes, generates attention and incorporates new attention-level supervision without retraining. Its second component ranks examples and features according to their negative impacts. This prioritization directs feedback toward corrections intended to produce large improvements with relatively little human effort, rather than requiring exhaustive inspection.

Experiments use time-series datasets from healthcare, real estate, and computer vision. The framework significantly outperforms the evaluated alternatives using conventional attention or omitting the cost-effective ranking procedure, while substantially reducing retraining and interaction costs. The findings support treating efficient human correction as a joint problem: the model must absorb feedback cheaply, and the interaction process must identify useful opportunities for correction.
icml-2020-cost-effective-interactive-att.tldr: Neural Attention Processes absorb human attention corrections without retraining, while impact-based prioritization reduces the feedback needed in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Estimating a property of an unknown distribution often starts by replacing its probabilities with observed frequencies. This paper develops estimators that extract more accuracy from the same observations. The amplification is statistical: using a given sample size, the new estimators match the accuracy that empirical-frequency estimators would obtain with substantially more samples.

For Shannon entropy and a broad class of Lipschitz properties, including L1 distance to a fixed distribution, n samples achieve the accuracy of the empirical estimator using n log n samples. For support size and coverage, the amplification factor instead depends logarithmically on the property value. The proposed estimators can also be computed in linear time.

These guarantees hold separately for every underlying distribution, making them stronger than a comparison restricted to worst-case distributions. The authors further establish that the logarithmic amplification factors are optimal. Experiments across many distributions show improvements over earlier estimators tailored to individual properties. The contribution combines computational efficiency with a distribution-by-distribution account of how much more effectively observations can be used.
icml-2020-data-amplification-instance-op.tldr: Linear-time estimators match empirical-frequency estimators using logarithmically more samples, with optimal amplification guarantees for every underlying distribution.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how unsupervised representation learning can reduce the number of labels needed for image recognition. Its motivating hypothesis is that recognition becomes more data-efficient when representations make variation in natural signals easier to predict. The authors revisit Contrastive Predictive Coding and improve its implementation to learn features guided by this objective.

The learned features support state-of-the-art linear classification accuracy on ImageNet in the reported evaluation. The authors also feed these representations into deep nonlinear classifiers. In that setting, classifiers need two to five times fewer labels than classifiers trained directly from image pixels, showing that the representation remains useful beyond a simple linear prediction stage.

The evaluation extends to object detection on PASCAL VOC, where the unsupervised representation substantially improves transfer and surpasses fully supervised ImageNet-pretrained classifiers. Together, the results support the practical value of learning predictive structure before training a labeled recognition model. They provide evidence for the motivating hypothesis through classification efficiency and transfer performance, without establishing it as a universal explanation of recognition.
icml-2020-data-efficient-image-recogniti.tldr: Improved Contrastive Predictive Coding learns image features that reduce label requirements and improve transfer to object detection in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning in games where agents choose from continuous action spaces and observe rewards only after delays. Feedback can arrive asynchronously and out of order, with no predetermined upper bound on its delay. Motivated by advertising and recommendation, the setting captures decisions whose consequences are not immediately available to the decision-maker.

The agents follow a no-regret learning policy while remaining unaware of the game structure and their opponents’ objectives. The proposed policy uses payoff observations rather than gradients. As reward information arrives, it enters a priority queue, giving the algorithm a mechanism for handling an irregular stream of feedback.

Under a standard diagonal concavity assumption, the authors prove that the resulting sequence of play converges to a Nash equilibrium with probability one, even when delays are unbounded. The assumption is central to the conclusion. The result shows that sufficiently structured continuous games can reach equilibrium despite severely delayed feedback, connecting individual learning rules to the eventual behavior of the interacting system.
icml-2020-gradient-free-online-learning-.tldr: Under diagonal concavity, a payoff-based learning policy converges almost surely to Nash equilibrium despite asynchronous feedback and unbounded reward delays.

paragraphs: Graph classification requires turning information about individual nodes into a representation of the whole graph. This paper introduces a new readout operation for that step. Its design uses persistent homology, bringing information about graph structure into the aggregation of node features rather than treating the readout solely as a combination of feature values.

The persistent homology computation is controlled by a learnable function that assigns real-valued filter values. Learning this function allows the structural summary to adapt to the classification problem. The authors establish a theoretical foundation for differentiating through the persistent homology computation, making this component available to gradient-based learning.

Empirically, the resulting readout compares favorably with earlier techniques, particularly when graph connectivity is informative for classification. This qualification explains where its structural emphasis is especially useful: the arrangement of connections must help distinguish the graphs. The contribution links a topological description of structure to a trainable graph-level representation, with both differentiation theory and classification experiments supporting the approach.
icml-2020-graph-filtration-learning-3b47.tldr: A differentiable persistent-homology readout learns graph-level representations that perform favorably, especially when connectivity helps determine graph classes.

paragraphs: Learning long-range behavior can be expensive for agents with complex bodies and many control dimensions. This paper investigates transferring knowledge from a simpler body to a more complex one. It separates control into an independently learned low-level policy and a high-level policy designed to transfer between agents with different morphologies.

Differences between bodies can make direct high-level transfer work poorly. The authors address this by encouraging the complex agent’s low-level controller to imitate the simpler agent’s low-level behavior. They show that this significantly improves zero-shot high-level transfer. A second component applies KL-regularized training to the high-level policy, which stabilizes learning and prevents mode collapse in the studied setting.

Experiments on navigation and manipulation environments demonstrate hierarchical transfer for long-range tasks across morphologies. The approach matters because it identifies an adaptation point below the transferred policy: improving compatibility between low-level behaviors can make high-level knowledge more reusable. The findings support the authors’ proposal that learning with a simpler agent can improve the sample efficiency of a more complex agent.
icml-2020-hierarchically-decoupled-imita.tldr: Low-level imitation and regularized high-level learning improve the transfer of long-range control policies between agents with different bodies.

paragraphs: Neural networks can memorize incorrect training labels, and familiar regularizers do not reliably prevent that behavior. This paper studies memorization through the information stored in network weights. It treats the weights as random variables influenced by both training data and training randomness, then measures their mutual information with the training labels while conditioning on the inputs.

The authors show that, for any training algorithm, lower values of this information quantity correspond to less memorization of label noise and better generalization bounds. This supplies a theoretical target for training. The quantity concerns how much label information the weights retain once the input examples are already accounted for.

To pursue that target, the proposed algorithms use an auxiliary network to predict gradients for the classifier’s final layers without accessing labels. The authors illustrate effectiveness on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 with several label-noise models, and on the naturally noisy Clothing1M dataset. The contribution connects an information-based account of memorization to a concrete modification of how classifier updates are generated.
icml-2020-improving-generalization-by-co.tldr: The paper links reduced label information in network weights to less noise memorization and proposes label-free gradient prediction to pursue that objective.

paragraphs: Model fusion aims to combine knowledge from experts whose training data and architectures remain private. Existing approaches can distill each expert’s predictions into an accessible imitator, then combine those imitators. The paper identifies a problem when experts solve different tasks: only some of the knowledge copied from each expert may be useful for a new task.

The proposed framework represents each expert as a distribution over predictive prototypes. It separates the prototypes from task-specific information, which is encoded in how the distribution allocates weight across them. This gives the fusion process reusable predictive components and a distinct representation of how those components relate to a particular task.

A new model can then be formed by recombining the task-agnostic prototypes according to a different distribution encoding the new task. Experiments on several real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the framework’s fusion and adaptation performance. The contribution is a way to organize black-box knowledge for selective reuse across tasks, rather than assuming that each expert’s complete predictive pattern transfers equally well.
icml-2020-learning-task-agnostic-embeddi.tldr: The framework separates reusable predictive prototypes from task-specific distributions so knowledge from multiple black-box experts can be recombined for new tasks.

paragraphs: Scientific simulators can generate observations even when the probability density of those observations cannot be evaluated tractably. This makes posterior inference difficult: the usual likelihood calculations are unavailable. The paper addresses this problem by learning an approximation to the likelihood-to-evidence ratio, avoiding a requirement to evaluate either of those quantities directly.

The learned estimator is amortized, allowing it to be reused across inference calculations. The authors embed it in Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers, where it approximates likelihood ratios between consecutive chain states. This provides a route to posterior sampling when the simulator’s likelihood is intractable, with the inference depending on the learned ratio approximation.

The work also presents methods for improving numerical stability and assessing approximation quality. Benchmarks against established techniques demonstrate the approach’s accuracy, while physics applications illustrate its scientific use. The key contribution is a reusable bridge between simulation and sampling: estimating the ratios needed by the inference procedure can make posterior inference feasible without a tractable likelihood model.
icml-2020-likelihood-free-mcmc-with-amor.tldr: A reusable learned likelihood-to-evidence ratio estimator enables approximate MCMC inference for simulators with intractable likelihoods.

paragraphs: This paper asks how accurately item qualities can be inferred from noisy pairwise comparisons. Comparisons follow a fixed graph: only neighboring items are compared, and each such pair is observed k times. Under the Bradley–Terry–Luce model, an item’s chance of beating another is its quality divided by the sum of their two qualities.

The analysis focuses on the regime where k is large. The authors determine the minimax estimation rate up to a constant factor, characterizing the best achievable worst-case expected error at that level of precision. This establishes a statistical target for learning the quality vector under the stated comparison model and graph structure.

They also show that a simple weighted least-squares algorithm reaches this rate. Its weights are determined by the observed comparison outcomes, and it can be implemented in time nearly linear in the total number of comparisons. The result therefore combines a characterization of achievable accuracy with a computationally efficient procedure that attains it in the analyzed large-comparison regime.
icml-2020-minimax-rate-for-learning-from.tldr: For many repeated comparisons on a fixed graph, an efficient weighted least-squares algorithm attains the BTL model’s minimax estimation rate up to constants.

paragraphs: Graphs and knowledge-based data describe discrete objects and their relationships, while many learning methods work with continuous representations. This paper introduces Nested SubSpace arrangement, or NSS arrangement, as a framework for connecting those forms of representation. The authors show that existing embedding techniques can be understood as members of this broader framework.

They use the framework to build Disk-ANChor ARrangement, abbreviated DANCAR, a representation-learning method designed to reproduce general graphs. This turns the unifying idea into a concrete embedding procedure. Its reconstruction objective makes preservation of the original graph relationships a central measure of whether the continuous representation is useful.

In the reported numerical experiments, DANCAR embeds WordNet into a 20-dimensional real-valued space and achieves an F1 score of 0.993 on graph reconstruction. The authors also identify visualization as a use of DANCAR for understanding graph characteristics. The contribution therefore spans a common description of embedding methods and a specific method with strong reported reconstruction performance on WordNet.
icml-2020-nested-subspace-arrangement-fo.tldr: NSS arrangement unifies embedding approaches, while its DANCAR implementation reconstructs WordNet with an F1 score of 0.993 in 20 dimensions.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems must cope with imbalanced data, limited recommendation slots, and users with different engagement patterns. The pAp@k metric combines partial AUC and precision at k to evaluate such systems. Conceptually, it asks how likely a highly ranked positive example is to outrank highly ranked negative examples, focusing evaluation on the top of the ranking.

Direct optimization is difficult because selecting top-ranked examples introduces a combinatorial structure. The authors analyze the metric’s learning-theoretic properties and construct surrogate objectives that are consistent under specified data regularity conditions. They then develop gradient-descent algorithms to optimize these surrogates, providing a practical route from the evaluation metric to model training.

The analysis and experiments suggest that pAp@k has a dual relationship with partial AUC and precision at k. The proposed methods outperform all evaluated baselines across the reported applications. These findings motivate its use for large-scale recommendation with heterogeneous engagement, while the consistency claim remains conditional on the stated regularity requirements.
icml-2020-optimization-and-analysis-of-t.tldr: The paper analyzes pAp@k and develops conditionally consistent surrogate objectives for training recommenders that emphasize the top of the ranking.

paragraphs: Choosing a composite kernel involves searching over discrete expressions, making the optimization difficult and preventing direct use of gradient methods on the original objective. Existing search approaches often narrow the candidate space to make the problem manageable. This can leave the result heavily dependent on expert choices about which structures should be considered.

DTERGENS approaches the problem by constructing and optimizing a generator of composite kernel expressions. The framework does not impose the candidate-space restrictions described for earlier approaches. It also jointly learns a termination criterion, allowing generated expressions to have flexible lengths instead of requiring a fixed expression size.

On many real-world prediction tasks, the authors report that the framework explores more diverse kernels and achieves better performance than the compared state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution is to make the production of candidate structures itself an optimization target. Learning both expression generation and when generation stops provides a way to search structures whose complexity can vary during the process.
icml-2020-optimizing-dynamic-structures-.tldr: DTERGENS learns a generator and stopping rule for variable-length composite kernels, improving search diversity and prediction in the reported tasks.

paragraphs: The paper develops a tractable, gradient-based parameterization of the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm for computing the rate-distortion function. This produces PARADISE, a framework for learning stochastic encoders. The framework is intended to support several learning settings, including supervised, semi-supervised, multi-task, and robust learning, through a flexible parameterized formulation.

The authors show that the PARADISE training objective can be interpreted as regularization that helps generalization. For robust learning, they introduce an additional posterior-matching objective that encourages smoothness in the loss function. This connects the encoder construction to two practical goals: better behavior on unseen data and greater resistance to adversarial perturbations.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet show significant improvements in interpretability and adversarial robustness. On CIFAR-10, the reported standard and adversarial error rates decrease by 50% and 41%, respectively, relative to the state-of-the-art comparison, without the expensive computational cost of adversarial training. These are experimental results for the evaluated setting, supporting the usefulness of the rate-distortion formulation as a learning objective.
icml-2020-parameterized-rate-distortion-.tldr: PARADISE turns rate-distortion optimization into a trainable stochastic encoder framework with reported gains in generalization, interpretability, and adversarial robustness.

paragraphs: In distributed empirical risk minimization, several machines calculate gradients while a central server updates the model. Repeated communication between them can be costly. This paper proposes an accelerated gradient method designed to reduce the number of communication rounds needed to reach a chosen accuracy by making additional use of data at the server.

The server solves a local optimization problem on a subsampled dataset to precondition the updates. The method’s convergence rate depends on the square root of the relative condition number between the global and local losses. This quantity captures how the local optimization problem relates to the global one, making their relationship central to the convergence analysis.

For linear prediction models, the authors bound this relative condition number by studying uniform concentration of Hessians over a bounded domain. The analysis yields improved rates for both existing preconditioned gradient methods and the proposed accelerated method. Experiments on real-world datasets illustrate acceleration’s benefits in ill-conditioned problems, linking the theoretical improvement to settings where optimization is difficult.
icml-2020-statistically-preconditioned-a.tldr: Server-side optimization on subsampled data preconditions an accelerated distributed method, improving convergence guarantees and showing benefits on ill-conditioned problems.

paragraphs: Stochastic Subspace Cubic Newton, or SSCN, is a randomized second-order method for minimizing high-dimensional convex functions. It connects two approaches: Newton-style updates with cubic regularization and stochastic descent within subspaces. This makes it both a stochastic extension of cubic Newton optimization and a curvature-aware enhancement of stochastic subspace descent.

The authors prove that changing the minibatch size moves the global convergence rate between those of stochastic coordinate descent and cubic regularized Newton. This gives a theoretical connection between first-order and second-order methods within one algorithm. The batch size controls where the method sits along that spectrum of convergence behavior.

Near the minimizer, SSCN’s convergence rate matches stochastic subspace descent on the quadratic defined by the objective’s curvature at that minimizer. Consequently, this local rate depends only on properties of the objective at the optimum. Numerical experiments show better performance than non-accelerated first-order coordinate descent and competitive performance with accelerated variants, supporting the practical promise of the theoretical connection.
icml-2020-stochastic-subspace-cubic-newt.tldr: SSCN combines randomized subspace updates with cubic Newton optimization, with convergence rates that bridge coordinate descent and second-order methods.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a neural network layer made from an ensemble of differentiable decision trees. Such trees can participate in gradient-based training, but existing versions are often slow because they do not support conditional computation. The authors aim to preserve differentiability while allowing computation to depend on the routes activated by each input.

A new sparse activation function controls sample routing, and specialized forward and backward algorithms exploit that sparsity. Together, these components implement conditional computation during both prediction and training. They make joint training of deep and wide tree ensembles feasible with first-order optimization methods such as stochastic gradient descent.

Across 23 classification datasets, experiments report speedups exceeding tenfold over earlier differentiable trees and more than twentyfold fewer parameters than gradient-boosted trees, with competitive performance. Replacing dense CNN layers on CIFAR, MNIST, and Fashion MNIST reduces test loss by 7–53% and parameter count eightfold. The authors also provide a TensorFlow implementation with a Keras interface, making the proposed layer available as a practical model component.
icml-2020-the-tree-ensemble-layer-differ.tldr: Sparse routing and specialized propagation make differentiable tree ensembles conditionally computed neural layers with substantial reported speed and parameter savings.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to regularize overparameterized neural networks when only a small training sample is available. It focuses on the internal representations immediately before a linear classifier. The proposed approach controls properties of the distribution in that representation space, shifting attention toward the geometry of learned features.

The authors impose a topological constraint on samples drawn from the probability measure induced in this space. They prove that the constraint produces concentration of probability mass around the representations of training examples. This supplies a mathematical link between the imposed structural condition and how the learned representation distribution is organized.

The paper identifies this concentration as beneficial for generalization and uses previous work to implement topological constraints in neural networks. Experiments across several vision benchmarks provide evidence for improved generalization. The contribution joins a theoretical concentration result with an empirical learning argument: shaping the representation distribution can be a useful form of regularization for networks trained with limited data.
icml-2020-topologically-densified-distri.tldr: Topological constraints on internal representations provably concentrate probability mass near training representations and empirically improve generalization in small-sample vision learning.

paragraphs: Concept drift occurs when the distribution generating observed data changes over time, potentially making a learned model inaccurate. Detecting it is difficult when data are high-dimensional, changes take different forms, or no suitable parametric model reflects the change. DAWIDD addresses this problem through a non-parametric approach to drift detection.

The paper’s central theoretical step establishes an equivalence between drift and dependence among specific random variables in the corresponding drift process. That reformulates detection as an independence-testing problem. The resulting method can look for evidence of distributional change without basing its decision on a parametric model or the loss of a particular classifier.

The authors describe the resulting scheme as fairly robust across different drift characteristics, with experiments supporting that assessment. Its significance lies in the statistical reformulation: a general test of dependence becomes a tool for recognizing changing data distributions. This supports detection across diverse kinds of change while keeping the evidence focused on the drift process itself rather than on one model’s predictive errors.
icml-2020-towards-non-parametric-drift-d.tldr: DAWIDD reformulates concept drift as statistical dependence, enabling non-parametric detection with reported robustness across diverse drift patterns.

paragraphs: ASVRCD is an accelerated form of stochastic variance-reduced coordinate descent. At each iteration it accesses only a random block of partial derivatives, making partial derivative access a defining feature of the method. It can handle objectives with a regularizer that is both nonsmooth and nonseparable, meaning the regularization need not split into independent terms for individual coordinates.

The method adds Nesterov’s momentum to the variance-reduced coordinate framework. The authors establish iteration-complexity guarantees that improve on those for SEGA and SVRCD, two related methods. This is a theoretical improvement in the number of iterations required, while retaining support for the stated broad class of regularizers.

The analysis also connects coordinate methods to finite-sum optimization, where an objective consists of many component terms. A variant of Katyusha appears as a special case of ASVRCD, recovering the optimal oracle complexity for that objective setting. This connection shows that the proposed framework encompasses an established accelerated finite-sum method as well as providing a new coordinate-descent algorithm.
icml-2020-variance-reduced-coordinate-de.tldr: ASVRCD adds momentum to variance-reduced coordinate descent, improves iteration guarantees, and recovers optimal finite-sum oracle complexity through a Katyusha special case.
